s15.title: Table S15. Evidence map of quantitative studies used for context.
rows: Causal effect of winning an ERC grant
Ghirelli, Havari, Meroni & Verzillo (2023), IZA DP 16108 / JRC
Sharp RDD at panel ranking cut-offs (multi-cutoff) + difference-in-differences
All ERC applicants 2007-2013 (StG and AdG); Scopus outcomes up to 9 years
No statistically significant effect of winning on productivity or quality near the threshold (exception reported: Physics in StG)
RDD around NIH R01 payline; near-miss vs narrow-win junior PIs
Near miss: >10% higher probability of leaving the NIH system; among those who persist, +6.1 percentage points probability of a top-5%-cited paper (p = 0.041); similar paper counts
Azoulay, Graff Zivin & Manso (2011), RAND Journal of Economics
Propensity-score weighting + difference-in-differences; HHMI investigators vs matched NIH-funded scientists

HHMI investigators produce high-impact papers at a much higher rate than NIH-funded controls (secondary summaries: roughly +39% publications, about +96% in the top-1% citation tier; 60-110% more high-impact papers); also more low-impact papers and more novel keywords
Schmaling & Gallo (2023), Research Integrity and Peer Review
Systematic review + meta-analysis of 55 studies (PROSPERO CRD42021232153)

Award acceptance 1% higher for men, not significant (95% CI: 3% more for men to 1% more for women), k = 36, I2 = 84%; reapplication acceptance 9% higher for men (95% CI 1-18%); smaller award amounts for women (g = -2.28)
Bornmann, Mutz & Daniel (2007), Journal of Informetrics
Men had about 7% greater odds of receiving a grant than women
Marsh, Bornmann, Mutz, Daniel & O'Mara (2009), Review of Educational Research
Multilevel re-analysis of the same 66 effect sizes
No robust gender effect once study dependencies are modelled (some estimates favour women)
verified 2026-09-06 (secondary citation in Science and Public Policy 2025)
Women: pooled RR 0.89 (95% CI 0.84-0.94) for grant success, absolute difference 3.2 pp, I2 = 58%; varies strongly by institute
Propensity-score weighting of successful vs unsuccessful applicants who reached the board stage
UK Medical Research Council early-career schemes, applicants 2006-2016 (n = 2,030)

Funded applicants of both genders secure more future funding; funded women receive more citations and are better cited in their field than unfunded women; no significant productivity/influence difference for men
Bajgar & Karapetyan (2025), IES Working Paper 30/2025, Charles University (revised Dec 2025; a 2026 journal version exists at ScienceDirect PII S016517652600056X but could not be accessed)
Augmented inverse probability weighting and regression discontinuity at the funding cutoff
Grants increase total publications over five years by about 2 papers (17%); RDD: first/last-author (PI-led) publications +1.8 papers (40%)
Single-rater intraclass correlation 0.259 (95% CI 0.249-0.279); higher in humanities, lower in biosciences
Cole, Cole & Simon (1981), Science; range as summarised by Cicchetti (1991) and cited in Hesselberg et al. (2025)
verified 2026-10-26 (Hesselberg et al. 2025 registered report protocol; the range is attributed there to Cicchetti 1991)
Norwegian funder (unnamed), as cited in Hesselberg et al. (2025), PLoS ONE 20(5):e0322696 (registered report protocol)
a Norwegian funder (not named in the citing source)
ICC about 0.29 even after an intervention to raise agreement; 6-15 reviewers would be needed to reach ICC 0.75 (Spearman-Brown)
Marsh, Jayasinghe & Bond (2008), American Psychologist (as cited)
Authors conclude funding decisions were based substantially on chance
Reliability of peer review (journals; context only)
ERC Scientific Council white paper (25 March 2026): Widening excellence - Bridging the ERC gap for a truly pan-European Research Area

Widening countries hold ~25% of EU population but about one-twentieth of ERC grants; success rates 1-7% vs ~11% average; in 2024, 940 applications from widening countries vs 7,271 from non-widening (11.4%)
verified 2026-10-26 (ERC news release and white paper PDF)
Jacob & Lefgren (2011), Journal of Public Economics
Fuzzy RDD at NIH priority-score payline
About one additional publication over five years (~7%) for marginal awardees
Bol, de Vaan & van de Rijt (2018), PNAS
Winners just above the threshold accumulate more than twice as much funding over the next eight years as near-losers; part of the gap arises because near-losers stop applying
